interest: This document provides valuable insight into how Allied wartime intelligence monitored Japan's home front and deteriorating economic conditions from diplomatic listening posts across the globe—London, Chungking, and Moscow. Because direct U.S. diplomatic reporting from Tokyo ceased after December 1941, American authorities relied on inter-allied intelligence exchanges with the British Ministry of Economic Warfare, Chinese intelligence gathered in Chungking, and Japanese press monitoring (specifically the Tokyo Asahi) conducted from the Soviet Union. The docket sheet also exemplifies State Department record-keeping practices and cross-referencing procedures for wartime economic intelligence during World War II.
overview: This file consists of a single Department of State 'List of Papers' (Form DS-46), dated October 12, 1945, cataloguing records classified under decimal file 894.5017 regarding the cost of living and domestic economic conditions in Japan during World War II. The sheet indexes three items received between October 1942 and February 1944 from American diplomatic missions in Great Britain, China, and the Soviet Union. These communications track third-country reporting and intelligence on Japanese wartime shortages, rationing regulations, and price controls, including a British Ministry of Economic Warfare report, observations on commodity scarcity from Chungking, and a Moscow telegram reporting on Tokyo press coverage of new ration cards for manufactured goods.

subfiles.about: A Department of State List of Papers indexing wartime reports from London, Chungking, and Moscow concerning Japan's cost of living, commodity shortages, and rationing.
subfiles.summary: This document is a Department of State List of Papers (Form DS-46) dated October 12, 1945, which indexes documents classified under decimal file 894.5017 (Cost of Living: Japan). It lists three wartime communications: an October 30, 1942 despatch (#6123) from Somerville in Great Britain transmitting a British Ministry of Economic Warfare paper on European rationing and Japanese deficiencies; an October 27, 1943 despatch (#1741) from Ambassador Clarence E. Gauss in Chungking enclosing an article on Japanese price control and commodity shortages; and a February 14 (1944) telegram (#2500) from Ambassador W. Averell Harriman in Moscow reporting a Tokyo Asahi announcement on new ration cards for manufactured goods. The document demonstrates how the State Department gathered and indexed external intelligence on Japan's wartime domestic economy after direct diplomatic relations were severed.
